entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Iakob Tsurtaveli, a pivotal 5th-century Georgian religious writer and priest, is primarily recognized as the author of "The Martyrdom of the Holy Queen Shushanik," a foundational work of early Georgian hagiography. Flourishing during a period when the Iberian Kingdom (modern-day Georgia) was solidifying its Christian identity against persistent Sasanian Persian Zoroastrian influence, Tsurtaveli's chronicle provided a powerful narrative of faith and resistance. His work not only established a cornerstone of Georgian literature but also served as a crucial historical document, illuminating the complex religious and political struggles that defined the South Caucasian region in late antiquity and contributing significantly to the cultural self-definition of a nascent Christian state.

Composed between 476 and 483 CE, "The Martyrdom of the Holy Queen Shushanik" details the persecution and death of Queen Shushanik, wife of Varsken, the ruler (Pitiakhsh) of Gogarene, a border region between Iberia and Armenia. Shushanik, an Armenian princess and devout Christian, refused to convert to Zoroastrianism after her husband, seeking favor with the Sasanian court, apostatized. Tsurtaveli, serving as Shushanik's confessor and a direct witness to many of these events, meticulously documented her steadfast faith, suffering, and eventual martyrdom at Tsurtavi. His narrative is notable for its vivid portrayal of court intrigue, theological debate, and the brutal enforcement of Sasanian religious policy, offering unparalleled insight into the social and spiritual fabric of 5th-century Iberia.
